# Qwen3-8B (LLM, Qwen3ForCausalLM decoder-only causal LM served via vLLM on ROCm) - MI300X Standalone Analysis

## Executive Summary

This trace captures a steady-state prefill-dominated serving step for Qwen3-8B on a single MI300X rank under vLLM. Over the 841.57 ms profiled window the GPU executes kernels for only 145.66 ms (17.31%) and sits idle for 695.85 ms (82.68%). Collective communication is absent and memory copies total 0.053 ms, so neither data movement nor collectives explain the idle time — it is host-side in origin, with 764.67 ms of host operator duration against 145.72 ms of device kernel time across 1072 launches. Within the compute that does run, GEMM dominates at 116.418 ms (79.93% of compute time), with the BF16 decoder linear layers sustaining 60-80% of the 708 TFLOPS matrix roofline; Paged Attention is a distant second at 12.0 ms but runs at only 13-15% of roofline. The largest available lever is therefore the host-side launch pipeline, followed by GEMM tile/precision tuning.

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| Total Time | 841.57 ms |
| Compute % | 17.31% |
| Idle % | 82.68% |
| Exposed Communication % | 0.00% |
| Top Bottleneck Category | GEMM (79.93%) |

![Performance Improvement](data:image/png;base64,)

### 🔴 P1: BF16 decoder GEMMs run at 60-80% of the compute roofline (Tensile)

**Insight**: The six largest BF16 linear-layer GEMMs in the Qwen3 decoder consume 108.2 ms of GPU kernel time while achieving only 60-80% of the 708 TFLOPS BF16 matrix roofline.

**Action**: Profile the dominant Tensile assembly kernels for tile-size and wave-occupancy tuning, starting with the 45.0 ms gate/up-projection GEMM at 69.86% of roofline. If the model tolerates a narrower precision than BF16, moving these unquantized linear layers to FP8 raises the compute ceiling from 708 to 1273 TFLOPS and lowers the compute floor for the same shapes.

### 🟡 P2: Paged Attention prefill kernel far below compute roofline

**Insight**: Both Paged Attention shapes sustain only 15.29% and 12.76% of the 708 TFLOPS bf16 matrix roofline, with the chunked-prefill forward kernel accounting for ~96% of the time in each.

**Action**: Profile the dominant `_fwd_kernel` component for tile-size and block-size tuning at query lengths 3073 and 1024. Enable chunked prefill to bound per-step latency for the prefill-dominated shape, and confirm the kernel handles the 4:1 GQA head grouping efficiently rather than replicating KV heads.

## System-Level Optimizations

> **Note:** System-level analysis is exploratory. The patterns and recommendations below are under active development and may be refined as system-level analysis matures.

Findings from system-level analysis (GPU utilization, memory transfer patterns,
communication/compute overlap). These affect the GPU pipeline as a whole.

### 🔴 P1: Capture the steady-state step in a GPU graph

**Insight**: Per-launch host dispatch cost leaves the device idle for 577 µs on average between the 1072 kernels in the window.

**Action**: Capture the steady-state forward step into a GPU graph and replay it each iteration, so one host-side submission drives the whole step instead of 1072 individual launches. Make shapes and buffer addresses static across iterations first, since graph capture requires them.

**Impact**: Not quantifiable from trace data
<!-- impact-end -->

### 🟡 P2: Remove blocking host-device synchronization from the hot path

**Insight**: 61 of 70 operator signatures spend more than five times their kernel duration on the host, which is the signature of the host waiting on the device rather than running ahead of it.

**Action**: Audit the attention, normalization and activation call sites for host-side reads of device tensors and for explicit device synchronization, and replace them with asynchronous equivalents or hoist them out of the per-layer loop. Keep host-to-device transfers non-blocking and on pinned memory so the host can queue the next layer while the current one runs.

<!-- impact-begin kind=p_item low=null mid=null high=null -->
**Impact**: Not quantifiable from trace data

### 🟢 P3: Reduce launch count in the small-kernel tail

**Insight**: 710 of 1072 launches deliver only 17.29 ms of device time, so two thirds of the dispatch cost buys under 12% of the useful work.

**Action**: Widen the compiled regions so normalization, activation and copy operators are emitted as fused kernels instead of separate launches, and fold residual-add plus normalization into the single fused operator already available in the kernel library. Fewer, larger kernels amortize the fixed per-launch cost that P1 and P2 cannot remove entirely.

### 🟢 P4: Memory copies run fully serialized against compute (sub-threshold, monitor only)

**Insight**: Every one of the 16 memory-copy events in this window is exposed rather than overlapped, giving a memcpy/compute overlap ratio of 0.0%, but the total transfer cost is only 0.053 ms out of 841.57 ms (0.01%), so it is not a current bottleneck.

**Action**: Leave the transfer path as-is at this scale; if transfer volume grows with batch size or sequence length in a future configuration, move these copies onto a dedicated copy stream backed by pinned host buffers so they proceed concurrently with the following compute kernels, which would raise the memcpy overlap ratio above 0% and drive exposed memcpy time toward zero.

### Compute Kernel Insights

#### 🔴 P1: BF16 decoder linear-layer GEMMs leave 20-40% of the compute roofline unused (Tensile)

**Identification:** Six GEMM signatures were flagged because each sustains less than the expected share of the BF16 matrix roofline while individually exceeding the impact threshold. All six are the same operation, the unquantized BF16 linear-layer GEMM inside the `Qwen3ForCausalLM` decoder stack, launched from the model's linear-layer utility helper and executed by the vendor GEMM library's Tensile assembly backend. The shapes correspond to the fused gate/up projection (N=24576), the down projection (K=12288), the fused QKV projection (N=6144), and the attention output projection (N=4096), at two different token-batch sizes (M=3073 and M=1024). Every one of these kernels is compute-bound, so the relevant ceiling is matrix throughput rather than bandwidth. (source: `gemm_metrics.json` → `category_findings[0].members[]`, `operations[].efficiency.efficiency_percent`, `operations[].efficiency.bound_type`, `operations[].library`, `operations[].module_chain`)

**Data:**

|-----------|--------|-----------------------------------------|-------------|-----------|------|-------|----------|------------|-------|

**Reasoning for Slowdown:** Every flagged kernel has an arithmetic intensity between 768 and 1639 FLOPS/Byte, far above the compute-bound threshold of 200, so bandwidth is not the limiter. Measured throughput ranges from 426 to 569 TFLOPS/s against a 708 TFLOPS BF16 ceiling, which is the 60-80% roofline band rather than the 85%+ expected of well-tuned large GEMMs. The largest contributor is the fused gate/up projection at M=3073, N=24576, K=4096, which alone costs 45.0 ms of kernel time at 69.86% of roofline. The same projection at the smaller M=1024 token batch drops to 66.82%, and the down projection at M=1024 drops further to 60.22%, so the gap widens as the M dimension shrinks and there is less work to spread across waves. The trace shows only the selected Tensile kernel name and its duration. Tile size not visible — profile the kernel for tile-size tuning. Kernel running slower than expected — profile occupancy with hardware counters.

**Resolution:** These GEMMs are already issuing a single fused kernel per call with no epilogue overhead to remove, so the remaining time comes from how the library partitions the problem across compute units. Retuning the tile shape changes how many workgroups the problem decomposes into, which directly determines whether the last wave leaves compute units idle — the shapes that fall furthest below roofline are exactly the small-M ones where a tile that is too tall wastes rows. Separately, all six operations run unquantized in BF16 while the hardware executes FP8 matrix instructions at 1273 TFLOPS versus 708 TFLOPS for BF16. Narrowing the precision halves the number of matrix-instruction issues needed for the same M×N×K product, which lowers the achievable floor for these kernels rather than merely closing the gap to the current one. Decomposition strategy not visible — profile the kernel for tiling layout.

**Resolution:** Tile-size and block-size tuning of the chunked-prefill forward kernel raises
the fraction of each wave's matrix-unit cycles spent on useful MFMA work, which directly
converts the measured 12-15% roofline occupancy into shorter kernel time at identical FLOP
count. Enabling chunked prefill splits a long prefill into bounded segments, which keeps
per-step latency predictable and lets the scheduler overlap prefill segments with decode
work instead of serializing behind one long kernel. Confirming that the kernel exploits the
4:1 GQA grouping matters because a kernel that materializes or re-reads KV heads once per
query head performs four times the KV traffic the layout actually requires. Root causes
beyond these are not determinable from a trace — generate a reproducer for the kernel team.

### System-Level Insights

<a id="detailed-analysis-system-p1"></a>
<!-- reasoning-candidate tier=system rank=1 -->
#### 🔴 P1: Per-launch host dispatch cost leaves the device idle between kernels

**Identification:** The device is idle for 82.68% of the captured window while
communication and memory copies together account for 0.01% of it, so the idle
time cannot be attributed to data movement. Summing the host-side durations of
every operator in the trace gives 764.67 ms against 145.72 ms of device time for
the kernels those operators launch. The window contains 1072 kernel launches, all
issued from the decoder stack of the traced causal language model. Spreading the
618.95 ms host excess over those launches gives 577 µs of dead device time per
launch (source: `cpu_idle_metrics.json` → `gpu_utilization.idle_time_percent`,
`category_manifest.json` → `categories[].gpu_kernel_time_ms`,
`categories[].cpu_duration_ms`).

**Data:**

| Metric | Value | Flagged |
|--------|-------|---------|
| Idle time | 695.9 ms (82.7%) | true |
| Computation time | 145.7 ms (17.3%) | true |
| Communication time | 0.0 ms (0.0%) | false |
| MemCpy time | 0.1 ms (0.0%) | false |
| Host operator duration in excess of kernel time | 619.0 ms (88.9% of idle) | true |
| Average host-side excess per launch | 0.6 ms | true |

**Reasoning for Slowdown:** The device finishes each kernel long before the host
submits the next one. Host operator duration covers 90.9% of the window while
device kernels cover 17.3%, so the host is the pacing resource and the device
waits on it. With 1072 separate submissions in the step, the fixed per-submission
cost is paid 1072 times and accumulates into 618.95 ms of bubbles. Neither
collective communication nor memory copies appear in the trace in any meaningful
quantity, which rules out data movement as the cause.

**Resolution:** Graph capture records the whole sequence of launches once and
replays it as a single host-side submission. The per-launch dispatch cost is then
paid at capture time rather than on every iteration, so the bubbles between
kernels collapse and the device queue stays fed. The trade-off is that captured
graphs require static shapes and stable buffer addresses, so the batch and
sequence dimensions must be padded to a fixed set of buckets before capture.

**Impact estimate:** Impact estimate is not quantifiable from trace data.

<a id="detailed-analysis-system-p2"></a>
<!-- reasoning-candidate tier=system rank=2 -->
#### 🟡 P2: Host-side synchronization prevents the host from running ahead of the device

**Identification:** 61 of the 70 distinct operator signatures in the trace spend
more than five times their kernel duration on the host. The largest offenders sit
in the attention path, the normalization path and the fused activation path of
the decoder layers. The attention operator spends 135.7 ms of host time beyond
its kernels across 72 invocations, which is 1.9 ms of host stall per call. The
fused add-and-normalize operator adds 84.5 ms across 144 invocations, and the
fused activation kernel adds 60.2 ms across 72 invocations (source:
`category_manifest.json` → `categories[].sync_time_ms`,
`categories[].sync_ops_count`, `categories[].has_sync_bottleneck`).

**Data:**

| Metric | Value | Flagged |
|--------|-------|---------|
| Operator signatures with host duration > 5x kernel time | 61 of 70 | true |
| Attention host time beyond kernels | 135.7 ms | true |
| Normalization host time beyond kernels | 180.2 ms | true |
| Fused activation host time beyond kernels | 97.2 ms | true |
| Elementwise host time beyond kernels | 105.1 ms | true |
| GEMM host time beyond kernels | 34.0 ms | true |

**Reasoning for Slowdown:** A healthy pipeline lets the host queue several
iterations of work ahead of the device, so the host cost per operator is hidden.
Here the host cost is fully exposed on almost every operator signature, which
means the host is blocking rather than queueing. The pattern is uniform across
attention, normalization, activation and elementwise operators, so it is a
property of the dispatch path rather than of one kernel. GEMM shows the smallest
relative gap because its kernels are long enough to cover part of the host cost.

**Resolution:** Each blocking host-side read of a device tensor drains the queue
and forces the device to go idle until the host refills it. Replacing those reads
with asynchronous equivalents, or moving them outside the per-layer loop, lets
the host stay ahead of the device so that submission cost overlaps with execution
instead of serializing against it. Non-blocking transfers from pinned host memory
preserve that overlap for any host data the step still needs.

**Impact estimate:** Impact estimate is not quantifiable from trace data.

<a id="detailed-analysis-system-p3"></a>
<!-- reasoning-candidate tier=system rank=3 -->
#### 🟢 P3: Two thirds of launches produce under an eighth of the device work

**Identification:** The trace contains 1072 kernel launches producing 145.72 ms
of device time, but 710 of those launches come from normalization, fused
activation, elementwise and miscellaneous operators that together produce only
17.29 ms. The two general matrix multiply and attention paths account for the
remaining 362 launches and 128.4 ms. The small-kernel operators all belong to the
repeated decoder layers of the traced model, so the launch count scales with
depth (source: `category_manifest.json` → `categories[].ops_count`,
`categories[].gpu_kernel_time_ms`, `ops_summary_by_category.csv` → `Count`).

**Data:**

| Metric | Value | Flagged |
|--------|-------|---------|
| Total kernel launches | 1072 | true |
| Launches in the small-kernel tail | 710 (66.2%) | true |
| Device time from the small-kernel tail | 17.3 ms (11.9%) | true |
| Normalization launches / device time | 290 launches, 8.1 ms | true |
| Fused activation launches / device time | 136 launches, 4.9 ms | true |
| Elementwise launches / device time | 173 launches, 2.2 ms | true |
| GEMM launches / device time | 290 launches, 116.4 ms | false |

**Reasoning for Slowdown:** Each of these 710 launches costs the same fixed host
dispatch work as a large matrix multiply, but returns two orders of magnitude
less device time. The normalization operators average 28 µs of device time per
launch and the elementwise operators average 13 µs, which is short enough that
dispatch cost dominates end-to-end time for those operators. Because the pattern
repeats once per decoder layer, the count grows with model depth and the overhead
grows with it.

**Resolution:** Fusing adjacent small operators into a single kernel removes one
dispatch per fused pair and also removes the intermediate write-back and re-read
between them, so both host cost and device bytes moved go down. Folding the
residual add into the normalization kernel is the highest-count instance of this
pattern in the trace. This reduction is complementary to graph capture, which
lowers the cost of each launch but does not reduce how many there are.

**Impact estimate:** Impact estimate is not quantifiable from trace data.

<a id="detailed-analysis-system-p4"></a>
<!-- reasoning-candidate tier=system rank=4 -->
#### 🟢 P4: Memory copies run fully serialized against compute (sub-threshold, monitor only)

**Identification:** The system-level scan compared when memory-copy activity occurs against when compute kernels occupy the device. None of the 16 copy events in the profiled window fall inside a compute window, so the measured overlap between copies and compute is zero percent. The same scan found no collective communication activity at all on this rank, which leaves communication blocking and communication overlap undefined rather than merely healthy. The copies themselves carry no direction tag and no byte count in the trace, so they cannot be attributed to a device-to-host, host-to-device, or device-to-device pattern (source: `multi_kernel_metrics.json` → `overlap_analysis.memcpy_overlap_ratio`, `memcpy_summary.by_direction`, `nccl_summary.total_count`).

**Data:**

| Metric | Value | Flagged |
|--------|-------|---------|
| Total GPU Timeline Window | 841.6 ms | false |
| Computation Time | 145.7 ms (17.3%) | false |
| Total Memcpy Events | 16 | false |
| Exposed Memcpy Time | 0.1 ms (0.0%) | false |
| Memcpy/Compute Overlap | 0.0% | false |
| Exposed Communication | 0.0 ms (0.0%) | false |
| Compute/Comm Overlap | Not measurable (no communication events) | false |

**Reasoning for Slowdown:** The zero overlap ratio is a real serialization signal, but its cost is bounded by the total transfer time of 0.053 ms. That is one hundredth of one percent of the 841.57 ms window, so removing the serialization entirely would not change end-to-end time. The dominant gap in this trace is that compute occupies only 17.31% of the window. That gap is not explained by data movement or by collective communication, both of which are effectively absent, and it therefore belongs to the host-side pipeline rather than to any multi-kernel pattern.

**Resolution:** Issuing the copies on a dedicated copy stream with pinned host staging lets the copy engine run concurrently with the compute pipeline instead of occupying a serialization point in the same stream. Pinned buffers also remove the staging bounce that forces a synchronous path for pageable memory. Neither change is worth making at the current 0.01% share; the value of the mechanism is as a guard for configurations where transfer volume scales up with batch size or sequence length.

**Impact estimate:** Impact estimate is not quantifiable from trace data.
